big_idea: Patterns can repeat, grow, or shrink — we can spot all three kinds in our classroom and our world.
learning_intention: We are learning to identify patterns as repeating, growing, or shrinking and to describe what changes from one term to the next.
student_learning_goal: I can identify a pattern as repeating, growing, or shrinking and describe what changes from one term to the next.
success_criteria: I can sort three example parades into the right pattern type (repeating, growing, shrinking).
I can describe what changes from term 1 to term 2 in a pattern.
I can find one real-life pattern in our classroom or school and tell my partner which type it is.
lesson_specific_materials: Coco the Conductor puppet (already prepped from earlier units, or freshly printed)
Class anchor chart paper labelled 'Pattern Parade — The Three Types'

Pre-built example parades for the opening reveal: (1) repeating Bea-Finn-Bea-Finn-Bea-Finn, (2) growing 1-Bea, 2-Bea, 3-Bea, 4-Bea (4 cells with 1, 2, 3, 4 Bea cards stacked), (3) shrinking 5-Bea, 4-Bea, 3-Bea, 2-Bea (4 cells)
Class diagnostic checklist (provided in assessment_suite stage)
PATTERN word card from M6 ready to tape on the chart; teacher hand-prints GROWING and SHRINKING beside it
Real-life pattern photos / examples for the hunt: classroom calendar, hopscotch grid, brick wall, stair photo, snowflake

minds_on.hook: Coco brought THREE different parades today. They look different — and Coco says they are different KINDS of patterns. Our job is to figure out the three kinds.
minds_on.teacher_script:
Bring children to the carpet in a circle. Hold up Coco. Say to students: 'Welcome back, parade builders! Last year — or in Grade 1 next door — we learned about repeating patterns. Coco taught us rules like AB and ABB. This year, Coco has TWO new tricks. Let me show you.'

Lay parade 1 (repeating Bea-Finn-Bea-Finn-Bea-Finn). Read with the class. Ask: 'What kind of pattern is this?' (repeating). Tape the PATTERN card to the chart and write REPEATING beside it.

Lay parade 2 (1 Bea, 2 Beas, 3 Beas, 4 Beas across 4 cells). Read with the class — count the Beas in each cell. Ask: 'Is this repeating? What is happening?' Children will say 'getting bigger' or 'one more each time.' Validate. 'This is a GROWING pattern. Each TERM gets BIGGER by the same amount. Today the rule is: add one Bea every term.' Hand-print GROWING on the chart.

Lay parade 3 (5 Beas, 4 Beas, 3 Beas, 2 Beas). Read with the class. Ask: 'What's happening here?' (getting smaller, one less each time). 'This is a SHRINKING pattern. Each term gets SMALLER by the same amount. The rule is: subtract one Bea every term.' Hand-print SHRINKING. 'Today's job: spot all THREE kinds in real life.'
student_actions: Sit in a circle on the carpet, facing the three example parades.
Read each parade aloud with the teacher and count the animals in each term.
Predict what type of pattern each parade is before the teacher names it.
Repeat the new words 'term', 'growing pattern', and 'shrinking pattern' aloud as a class.

steps.instruction: Whole-group sorting demo: lay out three more pre-built parades (one of each type) and three small chart-paper labels: REPEATING, GROWING, SHRINKING. Invite three children to come up, pick a parade, and place it under the correct label, explaining why.
steps.teacher_prompt: Say to students: 'Coco needs sorters. Three parades, three labels. Who wants to come up and sort one? You have to tell us WHY you chose that label — point to the terms and tell us what is happening.' After each child places one, ask the class: 'Does everyone agree? Anyone want to add why?'

steps.instruction: Partner build: each pair gets one set of Animal Cards (M1) and one Parade Strip (M2). Their job: build ONE example of each pattern type using the strip — first repeating across 5 cells, then a growing pattern across 4 cells (1 animal, 2 animals, 3 animals, 4 animals stacked in each cell), then a shrinking pattern across 4 cells. After each one, the partner names the type.
steps.teacher_prompt: Say to students: 'You and your partner are pattern builders. Build ONE repeating parade — partner names the type. Then build ONE growing parade by stacking more animals each cell. Then ONE shrinking parade. Tap your partner each time and say: "What kind?"'

steps.instruction: Real-life pattern hunt (10 min): pairs walk the classroom (and corridor if safe) with a clipboard. Their job: find at least ONE example of each type — repeating, growing, shrinking — in the real world. Write or sketch each find on the clipboard, label the type, and write the rule.
steps.teacher_prompt: Say to students: 'Now we leave the carpet. You and your partner walk slowly. Look for THREE patterns — one of each kind. Look at the calendar (numbers go up by 1 — growing!). Look at the floor tiles (might be repeating). Look at the windows. Sketch it, name the type, write the rule. Back here in 10 minutes.'

steps.instruction: Whole-class share: pairs return to the carpet and share one find each. The teacher records on the anchor chart under REPEATING, GROWING, SHRINKING — building a class artifact of real-life examples for the rest of the unit.
steps.teacher_prompt: Say to students: 'Bring your clipboard back to the carpet. Each pair, share one find. I will write it on the chart so we have a class list of every pattern in our classroom.' After each share, ask: 'What is the rule for that pattern? How does it change from one term to the next?'

steps.instruction: Circulate during partner build and the hunt. Use the diagnostic checklist to record which children can identify each pattern type, who needs the rule scaffolded, and who already names rules in +N or -N notation.
steps.teacher_prompt: Stop at each pair during the build phase. Pick one child. Ask: 'What kind of pattern is this?' and 'How does it change from term 1 to term 2?' Note responses on the diagnostic checklist.

differentiation.for_emerging: Stay with the repeating type and one simple growing type (+1 Bea per term). Provide pre-built example parades on the desk for the child to label before building. Pair with a confident peer for the hunt.
differentiation.for_extending: After building one of each type, challenge the pair to invent a +2 growing pattern (term 1 = 2 Beas, term 2 = 4 Beas, term 3 = 6 Beas) AND a -2 shrinking pattern. On the hunt, look for a pattern that changes by more than 1 each step (like odd numbers on the calendar, or doubling).
differentiation.for_ell_or_iep: Provide a small reference card with three sketches (repeating ABAB, growing 1-2-3-4, shrinking 4-3-2-1) labelled in the home language if known. Allow pointing and gestures as valid responses. On the hunt, pair with a partner who can scribe.
differentiation.for_movement_learners: After each parade, the pair stands and ACTS OUT the pattern. Repeating: alternate two body movements. Growing: each term, add one body part touching the floor. Shrinking: each term, take one body part off the floor.

formative_check.what_to_look_for: Can the child correctly identify each pattern type? Can they describe what changes from term to term, even informally ('one more' / 'one less' / 'they take turns')? Can they invent their own growing or shrinking pattern? Do they spot real-life examples without being shown?
formative_check.how_to_record: Tick the appropriate column on the diagnostic checklist for each child as you circulate.
tracker_columns: Describes change from term to term

discussion_prompts: What was the MOST interesting real-life pattern you found today? What kind was it?
Did you find any pattern that was hard to label? Why was it hard?
If a pattern keeps growing, when does it stop? Or does it ever stop?
consolidation.exit_routine: On the way out the door, each child gives the teacher one example of each type — 'A repeating pattern is ___. A growing pattern is ___. A shrinking pattern is ___.' Teacher records who can do all three confidently versus who needs more practice.

assessment_in_this_lesson.evidence_collected: Class diagnostic checklist completed during the partner-build phase and the real-life pattern hunt. Captures baseline understanding of C1.1 — including the new Grade 2 markers of distinguishing growing from shrinking and recognizing real-life pattern contexts — before Lesson 2 introduces formal rule notation (+N / -N).
assessment_in_this_lesson.rationale: This is the unit's diagnostic moment. The data tells the teacher who already distinguishes the three pattern types, so they can group flexibly for Lesson 2 onward. Children who can spot real-life patterns unprompted are ready for Lesson 4 far-prediction; children who confuse the three types need a small-group re-loop before Lesson 2's growing/shrinking work.

expanded_walkthrough.title: The Three-Type Sort — when 'just bigger' becomes 'growing by N'
expanded_walkthrough.rationale: Step 2 (partner-build one example of each type) is the first place where G2 children must commit to the distinction between repeating, growing, and shrinking. Step 3 (real-life hunt) is where the abstraction is tested — children either find genuine examples of each type in the world, or they confuse 'lots of stuff' with 'growing.' The script below covers the three most common confusions during these two steps.
expanded_walkthrough.setup: Each pair has Animal Cards (M1), Parade Strip (M2), and a clipboard for the real-life hunt. Carpet anchor chart has three columns: REPEATING, GROWING, SHRINKING. Teacher carries the diagnostic clipboard with one row per child and three columns for each type-identification skill.
expanded_walkthrough.teacher_script:
Walk to a pair building the GROWING parade. They've placed Bea, Bea-Bea, Bea-Bea-Bea-Bea — increases of 0, 1, 2 (irregular). Stop them. 'Tell me your rule. Each parade gets bigger by HOW MUCH?' If they say 'a little bit each time,' that's confused. The G2 demand is a CONSTANT rule. Show: 'Watch me — Bea, Bea-Bea-Bea, Bea-Bea-Bea-Bea-Bea — +2 each time. The same +2 every time. Now you redo yours: pick ONE rule, like +1 or +2 or +3, and stick to it.'

Move to a pair building SHRINKING. They've built 6 Beas, 4 Beas, 1 Bea (irregular shrink). Same script: 'What's your shrinking rule? -2 then -3?' Pause. 'A shrinking pattern needs the SAME minus-rule every time. -2 then -2 then -2. Try again.' Many G2 children initially imagine 'shrinking' just means 'getting smaller however.' Forcing the constant rule is the conceptual lift.

During the real-life hunt: walk past a pair pointing at a row of identical lockers and saying 'this is growing.' Pause them. 'Tell me what's getting BIGGER. The lockers are all the same size. Is anything CHANGING from one locker to the next?' Wait. They'll either retract ('oh, this is REPEATING — same locker over and over') or argue that the row growing is bigger overall (still confused). Use this as a teaching moment for the whole class share at the end.

Stretch the strong children. Find a pair that has built all three types confidently. Hand them a sticky note. 'Write a +3 rule. Build a +3 growing parade. Then SAME +3 rule, but invent it for SHAPES instead of animals — circle, two circles, three circles. Same rule, different stuff.' Transfer across representations is your G2 marker for L4 evidence.
expected_student_responses: (Confused) Builds an irregular shrink/grow ('a little bit smaller each time'), can't articulate a constant rule.
(Mid) Names +1 or -1 confidently but treats +2 / +3 as exotic. Comfortable only with unit-step rules.
(Strong) Names +N rule explicitly, transfers to a different representation (shapes, sounds, body) without prompting.
(Stretched) Voluntarily invents a +0 or 'special case' rule as repeating, articulating that 'repeating is just growing-by-zero' — full conceptual integration.
common_misconceptions: Growing means 'getting bigger somehow' rather than 'getting bigger by the SAME amount each time.' (Children produce irregular increments and call them growing.)
Repeating, growing, and shrinking are visually different things, not the same RULE in different forms. (Children sort by surface appearance, not by examining the rule.)
A row of identical objects is growing because the row is getting longer. (Conflates the visible accumulation with the conceptual definition of growing.)
recovery_moves: Force the rule to be constant. Make children write the rule explicitly on a sticky (+1, +2, -2, etc.) BEFORE they build. Verbal commitment first, build second.
Use the +0 framing. 'Repeating is just growing by zero each step.' Some G2 children unify the three types this way; others find it confusing. Try it; if it sticks, it's the most powerful integration.
Real-life filter: ask 'is anything CHANGING from one to the next?' If no, it's repeating. If yes, by how much? Force the audit before they categorize.

worksheet_brief.purpose: Independent practice of C1.1 — identifying patterns as repeating, growing, or shrinking AND describing the change from one term to the next.

parts_outline.task: Show three pattern strips at the top: one repeating (Bea-Finn-Bea-Finn-Bea), one growing (1, 2, 3, 4 Beas across cells), one shrinking (4, 3, 2, 1 Finns across cells). Beside each strip, three label boxes: REPEATING, GROWING, SHRINKING. Student draws a line from each strip to the matching label.
Show a growing parade strip (4 cells with 2, 4, 6, 8 Beas — adding 2 each term). Below it, two writing lines: 'This is a ____ pattern.' and 'The rule is: add ____ each term.'

Real-life observation. Show 4 small thumbnail photos: a calendar week (1, 2, 3, 4...), a brick wall (alternating offset), hopscotch numbers (1, 2, 3, 4...), and a half-eaten cookie sequence (whole, 3/4, 1/2, 1/4 — shrinking). Student writes the type below each photo.
